Description

RKIP (Raf kinase inhibitor protein, PEBP1) binds RAF1, MEK and ERK but not RAS, and it inhibits the phosphorylation and activation of MEK by RAF1 [1]. Its binding to RAF1 and to MEK are mutually exclusive: RKIP takes MEK away from RAF1 and competes with MEK as the substrate of RAF1 [2]. Protein kinase C switches this brake off. Its phosphorylation of RKIP on Ser153 releases RKIP from RAF1, and the phosphorylated RKIP then binds and inhibits the G protein-coupled receptor kinase GRK2 [3]. One kinase thus lifts a brake on ERK signalling and, at the same time, prolongs signalling from G protein-coupled receptors, shown in heart muscle cells with β-adrenergic receptors [3].

References

  1. Yeung K, Seitz T, Li S, Janosch P, McFerran B, Kaiser C, et al. Suppression of Raf-1 kinase activity and MAP kinase signalling by RKIP. Nature. 1999;401(6749):173-7. PMID: 10490027. doi: 10.1038/43686.
  2. Yeung K, Janosch P, McFerran B, Rose DW, Mischak H, Sedivy JM, et al. Mechanism of suppression of the Raf/MEK/extracellular signal-regulated kinase pathway by the raf kinase inhibitor protein. Mol Cell Biol. 2000;20(9):3079-85. PMID: 10757792. doi: 10.1128/MCB.20.9.3079-3085.2000.
  3. Lorenz K, Lohse MJ, Quitterer U. Protein kinase C switches the Raf kinase inhibitor from Raf-1 to GRK-2. Nature. 2003;426(6966):574-9. PMID: 14654844. doi: 10.1038/nature02158.
